method.intro: Every number on the benchmarks page comes from one source and one formula. This page states both, plus the limits, so a figure can be checked or corrected rather than taken on trust.

method.method1: Daily output = reading speed × hours you run the machine.

method.method4: Payback days = rig price ÷ money saved per day versus an API.
method.assumptionsIntro: The table uses these defaults. Change any of them on the benchmarks page and every derived figure updates.
method.assumptionReadingShare: Share of output that is reading
method.limitsTitle: What these numbers do not cover
method.limit1: Consumer GPUs only. Server parts and multi-GPU configurations are excluded.
method.limit2: One workload: a sequential single-stream mix. Batched, concurrent serving runs faster in aggregate and slower per stream.
method.limit3: Prices are dated street prices and move independently of the measurements.
method.limit4: A payback figure is an estimate, not a quote: it assumes the machine is busy at the stated hours.
method.freshnessBody: The table was last synchronised on {date}. Measures are re-published in place, so a figure quoted from an older copy can be checked against its date.

vps.title: 2026 budget VPS deals: China-optimized routes and ~$20/year bandwidth
vps.intro: A daily-verified shortlist of affordable VPS plans for visitors in mainland China and for local AI relays or nodes. We look for about $20/year (up to about $30 when the route is clearly better), at least 100 Mbps, and honest notes on CN2 GIA, CMIN2, 9929, CUII, or optimized direct routes — regular international transit is never labelled as a premium China path.
vps.dailyNote: This page is refreshed from a data file, so a full site rebuild is not required every day. A Cloudflare 403 or other temporary block keeps the last good record and is never treated as a delisting; a vendor 404 is what marks a plan out of stock.
vps.criteriaBudget: Around $20/year, with a hard look at plans up to $25; clearly better premium routes may go up to about $30.
vps.criteriaBandwidth: High-bandwidth picks start at 100 Mbps. A 5 Mbps special stays in the footnotes even if the route is good.
vps.criteriaRoute: Prefer mainland-China-optimized routes (CN2 GIA / CMIN2 / 9929 / CUII / optimized direct) and say plainly whether China Telecom CN2 is present.
vps.criteriaUse: Intended for nodes that Chinese users will hit, local AI relays, or light services. Regular international plans are listed only as control-plane or non-China backups.
vps.dealsTitle: China-optimized high-bandwidth plans that are still orderable
vps.backupTitle: Regular international backups (control plane / non-China traffic)
vps.backupIntro: These often have more bandwidth and disk, and same-price renewals are more common, but they are not China-optimized routes.
vps.disclosure: Some checkout buttons already use approved affiliate or referral links (those links are marked rel=sponsored). Listings without an approved code still go to the official vendor page. We list plans by verified stock, price and route quality, and we will not hide a 5 Mbps cap or a non-optimized route for a commission. The price that matters is the one on the vendor checkout page; confirm renewal terms and datacenter stock before you pay. Outbound click records, when collected, only measure visits through our hop and are not orders or sign-ups.
vps.noDeals: No verified high-bandwidth plans are currently in stock.

faqs.question: Which VPS plans around $20 work well from mainland China?
faqs.answer: As of the 2026-11-13 check, there is almost no in-stock premium China-optimized plan at $20/year with 100 Mbps or more. The closest fits are DediOne’s Los Angeles/Kansas mainland-optimized 2C2G ($25.99/year, 200 Mbps unmetered, optimized direct) and DediOne Los Angeles CMIN2+CUII ($29.99/year, 200 Mbps, 500 GB/month). CloudCone and RackNerd plans at $14–22 have more bandwidth but use regular international transit. The $19.99 5 Mbps CMIN2 special is only for very light use.

faqs.question: What is the difference between CMIN2 and a regular 163 route?
faqs.answer: CMIN2 is China Mobile’s premium return path and is usually more stable than ordinary CMI/163 at peak hours; DediOne’s CMIN2 plans also add China Unicom CUII. A “163” or “optimized direct” line is often CN2 GT or plain direct peering, which typically lags CN2 GIA / CMIN2 / 9929 at night. Ignore marketing words and test the published IP from China Telecom, Mobile and Unicom yourself. This page always states whether China Telecom CN2 is present.

faqs.question: How do I test latency and the route back to mainland China?
faqs.answer: Ping or run mtr to the test IP from Telecom, Mobile and Unicom networks, then read traceroute for CN2 (59.43), CMIN2, 9929, or ordinary 163/CMI hops. After purchase, test your own IP the same way. Latency varies by province and time of day, so one sample is not a full-day guarantee.

faqs.question: Why is the 5 Mbps CMIN2 special not recommended?
faqs.answer: The DediOne Los Angeles CMIN2 special is about $19.99/year with a decent CMIN2+CUII path, but the cap is only 5 Mbps, which saturates quickly for relays or multi-user access. This page’s high-bandwidth bar starts at 100 Mbps, so that plan is listed only as a footnote.

faqs.question: Should I buy now or wait for Black Friday?
faqs.answer: If you do not need the servers immediately, the week around Black Friday 2026 (27 November) is when RackNerd, CloudCone, DMIT, HostDare and VMISS more often release same-price-renewal deals. In-stock premium lines at $20/year and ≥100 Mbps are scarce right now, so it is reasonable to watch this page and buy if a clearly better Black Friday offer appears.

faqs.question: Are these affiliate links, and are the prices guaranteed?
faqs.answer: Where an approved affiliate or referral code exists, the button goes to the vendor page with that code and stays disclosed here (rel=sponsored). Other buttons still go to official pages. Prices, stock and renewal terms are always those on the vendor checkout page. This list is checked daily, but it does not replace a last look before you pay.

canIRun.title: Can My PC Run a Local LLM? VRAM & RAM Calculator
canIRun.intro: Pick your GPU or enter your VRAM, system RAM, and target context length (8K–128K). Get an instant quantization verdict, KV-cache memory estimate, expected tok/s, and local cost vs API break-even.
canIRun.unifiedLabel: Unified memory (Apple Silicon / Strix Halo / DGX Spark)
canIRun.verdictCanRun: Yes — your hardware can run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next locally.
canIRun.verdictCannotRun: Not enough memory for the minimum 125B build yet.
canIRun.bottleneckVram: Dedicated GPU VRAM is below the 12 GB minimum floor. Upgrade to a 12 GB+ GPU (e.g., RTX 3060 12GB, RTX 5070, or RX 7900 XTX) or use a 64 GB+ unified-memory machine.
canIRun.bottleneckRam: Your GPU VRAM meets the 12 GB floor, but system RAM is below the 32 GB minimum (or too tight for this context length). Try 8K context or upgrade to 64 GB RAM.
canIRun.bottleneckUnified: Unified memory needs ~20% headroom for the OS. Aim for at least 48–64 GB unified memory (Mac mini M5 Pro 64 GB or Ryzen AI Max+ 128 GB).
canIRun.tierTableTitle: Quick reference: what each VRAM & RAM tier can run (at 32K context)
canIRun.tierTableIntro: Every row is computed directly from the same quantization floors and KV-cache rules as the interactive calculator above.
canIRun.tierFootnote: * Unified memory shares one pool with the OS (~82% usable for model + KV cache).
canIRun.faq1Q: What is the minimum GPU VRAM and RAM to run Strata locally?
canIRun.faq1A: You need at least 12 GB GPU VRAM and 32 GB system RAM for the Coder build, or 12 GB VRAM + 64 GB RAM for the recommended IQ2_XS default build.
canIRun.faq2Q: Can an 8 GB GPU like an RTX 4060 run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next?
canIRun.faq2A: No — 8 GB discrete VRAM sits below the 12 GB minimum floor for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next builds. Moving to a 12 GB or 16 GB card (such as RTX 4070, RTX 5070, or RX 9070 XT) unlocks local runs.
canIRun.faq3Q: How much extra memory does 128K context require?
canIRun.faq3A: Long 128K context adds roughly 14 GB of KV-cache memory overhead compared to ~1.5 GB at 8K context, so 64 GB–96 GB system RAM (or 128 GB unified memory) is recommended for heavy 128K workloads.
canIRun.faq4Q: Is Apple Silicon unified memory faster or slower than an RTX 4090?
canIRun.faq4A: Apple Silicon holds much larger models in one quiet unified pool (64–512 GB), while discrete NVIDIA cards like the RTX 4090 (109.3 tok/s) and RTX 5090 (168.4 tok/s) generate tokens 2–5× faster.
